items.p: What is living light?
opts: Light made by a living thing, using chemistry in its body
Sunlight shining on a living thing
Light from a lamp in a garden
Any light we see at night
items.why: Living light, or bioluminescence, is made by the living thing itself. Picking 'sunlight shining on it' mixes up making light with sending back light. A leaf in the sun is lit, but it does not make light.
items.art: A firefly glowing next to a leaf lit by the Sun, with a tick by the firefly.

items.p: A firefly is a kind of…
items.why: Fireflies are beetles. They have hard wing cases like all beetles. Picking 'fly' comes from the name, but names can fool us. Picking 'worm' may come from glow-worms, which are firefly young.

items.p: A firefly makes light when a chemical called luciferin meets the gas ____ from the air.
items.why: Oxygen from the air reacts with luciferin, and light comes out. The firefly switches its light on by letting air into its lantern.

items.p: A firefly's light is hot, like a candle flame.
items.why: False. Living light is cold light. It makes almost no heat, so the firefly does not burn itself.

items.p: Why do most fireflies flash?
opts: To find a partner of their own kind
To see where they are flying
items.why: Fireflies flash codes to find a partner. Picking 'to see where they are flying' treats the flash as a torch. Their flashes are messages. Picking 'keep warm' misses that firefly light is cold.

items.p: Match each glowing living thing to where it lives.
pairs: fields and gardens on warm nights
items.why: Living light is found on land, in forests and all through the sea.

items.p: You put one glow stick in icy water and one in warm water. Which glows brighter?
items.why: Warmth makes the chemicals react faster, so more light comes out each second. Picking 'icy water' may come from thinking cold things shine. Picking 'the same' may mean the room was too bright to see the difference.

items.p: A glow-in-the-dark star glows after you shine a torch on it. Does it make its own light?
opts: No, it gives back light it soaked up
items.why: The star stores light, then lets it out slowly. A firefly makes new light from a chemical reaction. Picking 'just like a firefly' mixes up glowing with making light.

items.p: Sort these. Does it make its own light, or not?
cats: Does not make its own light
items: a firefly
Makes its own light
the Moon
Does not make its own light
a glowing mushroom
Makes its own light
a mirror
Does not make its own light
an anglerfish's lure
Makes its own light
a white cat in torchlight
Does not make its own light
items.why: Light sources make their own light. The Moon, a mirror and a cat only send back light from something else. The anglerfish's lure is lit by bacteria living in it, which make light.

items.p: Deep in the sea, below about 1,000 metres, how much sunlight is there?
opts: Lots, the water makes it brighter
items.why: Sunlight fades as it goes down through water. Below about 1,000 metres it is completely dark, day and night. Picking 'a little at midday' is close for a few hundred metres down, but not for the deep sea.

items.p: Most animals in the deep sea can make their own light.
items.why: True. In one count of deep-sea animals off California, about three out of every four could glow.

items.p: Why does an anglerfish have a glowing ball on its head?
opts: To bring small fish close, so it can eat them
items.why: The glowing lure is bait. Small fish swim up to it and are swallowed. Picking 'to see in the dark' treats it as a headlamp. Picking 'to hide' mixes it up with belly lights.

items.p: Draw a firefly at night. Show where its light comes from. Draw an arrow for the air going in.
items.a: A beetle with its glowing lantern at the end of its body, with an arrow of air going into the lantern.
items.why: The light comes from the lantern, where luciferin meets oxygen from the air.

items.p: Why are bright lights at night bad for fireflies?
items.a: Fireflies flash to find partners. Bright lights hide their flashes, so males and females cannot see each other. Then fewer baby fireflies are born.
items.why: Light pollution is one of the biggest threats to fireflies, along with losing their homes.

items.p: Name two living things that make light, and say what each one uses its light for.
items.a: For example: a firefly flashes to find a partner. An anglerfish uses its glowing lure to catch small fish.
items.why: Any two correct living things, each with a job, are right.

items.p: Light made by living things is called bio____.
items.why: Bioluminescence means living light. Bio means life, and luminescence means giving out light.

items.p: What does the helper chemical luciferase do in a firefly?
opts: Makes luciferin and oxygen react quickly
items.why: Luciferase is a helper that speeds up the reaction, so the flash comes on fast. Picking 'stores sunlight' mixes living light up with glow-in-the-dark stars.

items.p: A firefly's light is cold light. Why does that matter for the firefly?
opts: A hot light would burn its own body
Cold light is brighter than any other light
Cold light can be seen in the daytime
It does not matter at all
items.why: A firefly's lantern is part of its body. A hot light would cook it. Picking 'brighter' is a mix-up: cold means 'makes little heat', not 'very bright'.

items.p: In the glow stick test, the warm glow stick was brightest. Next morning, which one was most likely still glowing?
opts: The one from the icy water
The one from the warm water
None ever glow for more than a minute
items.why: In the cold, the reaction runs slowly and uses up the chemicals slowly. The warm stick spent its chemicals fast. Picking 'warm' usually means thinking brighter means stronger and longer.

items.p: A hatchetfish glows on its belly. What is that light for?
opts: To hide its dark shape from hunters below
items.why: From below, a fish shows as a dark shape against the dim light above. Belly lights fill in the shape. Picking 'catch food' mixes it up with the anglerfish's lure.

items.p: Some jellyfish flash a ring of lights when they are grabbed. Scientists call this a burglar alarm. Why?
opts: The flashes may call a bigger hunter to eat the attacker
It turns off the attacker's eyes
items.why: Like an alarm, the flashes draw attention. A bigger animal may come and eat whatever grabbed the jellyfish. Picking 'turns off the attacker's eyes' is a guess, but no light can do that.

items.p: Where does an anglerfish's lure get its light?
opts: From glowing bacteria living inside it
items.why: Tiny glowing bacteria live in the lure. The fish gives them a home and food, and they give the fish its lamp. Picking 'the Sun' misses that sunlight never reaches the deep sea.

items.p: Glowing bacteria only light up when there are lots of them together.
items.why: True. They give off a chemical to tell each other they are there. When enough builds up, they all glow at once.

items.p: Iba, in the story The Lamps That Stay, got home by following the mushrooms, not the fireflies. Why?
opts: The mushrooms glowed steadily and stayed where they grew, by the stream
The fireflies were too hot to go near
The mushrooms were brighter than the Sun
items.why: Fireflies flash and move about, talking to each other. The mushrooms stay on old bamboo by the stream, glowing all night. Picking 'too hot' misses that firefly light is cold.
items.context: In the story The Lamps That Stay, two children are lost at night in a forest in Meghalaya. Fireflies flash all around them, and glowing mushrooms grow on fallen bamboo.

items.p: Put the steps of a firefly flash in order.
items: The firefly lets air into its lantern
Oxygen meets luciferin
Luciferase makes the reaction fast
Light comes out
The firefly stops the air, and the light goes off
items.why: Air brings oxygen. Oxygen reacts with luciferin, helped by luciferase. Light comes out. Shutting off the air stops the light.

items.p: A substance that soaks up light and gives it back slowly in the dark is called glow-in-the-____.
items.why: Glow-in-the-dark materials store light. They do not make new light, as fireflies do.

items.p: Glowing mushrooms flash on and off like fireflies.
items.why: False. Glowing fungi glow steadily, all night long, for as long as they are alive and damp.

items.p: Some female fireflies copy the answer flash of another kind. What happens when a male of that kind flies down?
items.why: The scientist James Lloyd found these trickster fireflies in 1965. They use light as a trap. Picking 'become friends' is kind, but nature is not always kind.

items.p: Match each deep-sea light to its job.
items.why: Deep-sea animals use light for four main jobs: to catch food, to hide, to scare attackers and to talk.

items.p: Why do you think so many deep-sea animals make light, but so few animals on land?
items.a: On land, the Sun lights the day, so many animals can see without making light. In the deep sea it is always dark, so light is the only way to see, signal or trick in the dark.
items.why: Any answer that links glowing to the darkness of the deep sea is good.

items.p: Raphael Dubois mixed two juices from a glowing beetle in a tube, and they glowed. What does this tell us about living light?
items.a: Living light comes from chemicals. It can even happen outside the animal's body, if the right chemicals and oxygen are mixed.
items.why: This experiment showed that living light is chemistry, not magic or a spirit.
items.context: In the 1880s, Raphael Dubois, a French scientist, made two juices from the glowing part of a click beetle. Neither glowed alone.

items.p: A firefly eats food and later makes light. Where did the energy in its food first come from?
items.why: Plants catch sunlight to make food. Animals eat plants, or eat animals that ate plants. So a firefly's flash is sunlight energy, changed many times. Picking 'from its light' goes the wrong way round. Light is where the energy ends up.

items.p: Down at the level of atoms, how does luciferin make light?
opts: The new molecule has extra energy and lets it go as tiny packets of light
It catches sunlight and holds it
Tiny lamps inside its atoms switch on
items.why: After luciferin reacts with oxygen, the new molecule is jumpy with extra energy. It calms down by giving out a photon, the tiniest bit of light. Picking 'catches sunlight' mixes it up with glow-in-the-dark stars. Picking 'catches fire' misses that there is no flame or heat.

items.p: Scientists think living light began only once, in one ancient animal, and was passed down to all glowing things.
items.why: False. Fireflies, fungi, jellyfish and bacteria use different chemicals. Scientists think living light began separately at least 94 times.

items.p: Scientists found that more insects landed on fake glowing mushrooms than on dark ones. What does this suggest?
opts: The glow may bring insects that spread the mushroom's spores
Insects are scared of the dark
It proves every mushroom glows for this reason
items.why: This test, in Brazil in 2015, suggests one reason for one kind of mushroom. Picking 'it proves every mushroom' goes too far. One test on one kind cannot tell us about all fungi.

items.p: Your grandmother says there were many more fireflies when she was a child. Is that good evidence that fireflies are disappearing? How could you find out for sure?
items.a: It is a useful clue, but memories can be wrong or patchy. To find out for sure, many people would need to count fireflies in the same places, at the same time, every year, and compare the counts.
items.why: Scientists say there are very few long counts of fireflies in India. Careful counts, like the firefly count project, help.

items.p: In the made-up firefly count, the three nights gave 24, 9 and 31 flashes. How many more flashes were there on the best night than the worst?
items.why: The best night had 31 and the worst had 9. 31 take away 9 is 22. Picking 7 subtracts the wrong nights. Picking 40 adds them instead of finding the difference.

chart.title: Made-up example: firefly flashes counted in 3 minutes

items.p: Osamu Shimomura found a protein in a jellyfish that glows green. How do scientists use it today?
opts: They attach it to parts of cells so those parts light up under a microscope
They put it in street lamps
items.why: The green protein lets scientists see where things are and how they move inside living cells. Shimomura shared a Nobel Prize for this in 2008.

items.p: Your body gives out a very faint light, about a thousand times too weak for your eyes to see.
items.why: True. In 2009, scientists in Japan photographed it with a super-sensitive camera in total darkness. What it can tell us is still being studied.

items.p: In the cold light test, your hand felt warm by the candle, but not by the glow stick. What does this show?
opts: The glow stick turns its energy into light, with almost no heat
The glow stick has no energy
Light and heat are always the same thing
items.why: Both make light, but the flame also makes a lot of heat. The glow stick, like a firefly, makes cold light. Picking 'no energy' misses that light itself is energy.

items.p: Design a light for a village path near a firefly field. Say two things you would do, and why.
items.a: For example: put a shade on top so the light points only down at the path. Use a dim, warm lamp, and switch it off late at night. This keeps people safe and leaves the field dark for fireflies.
items.why: Any two ideas that light the path but keep light away from the fireflies are good.

items.p: A deep-sea fish called a cookiecutter shark glows all over its belly, except for a dark collar. Scientists think the dark collar looks like a small fish from below. Why might that help the shark?
opts: Bigger fish swim up to bite the 'small fish', and the shark bites them instead
It shows the shark where the sea floor is
items.why: The dark patch may work as a lure, like the anglerfish's glow. Light and dark can both be used to trick. Picking 'keeps warm' misses that living light is cold.
items.context: A cookiecutter shark is a small shark that takes round bites out of bigger fish and whales.

items.p: The mushrooms in Meghalaya were known to local people long before scientists named them in 2020. Who do you think discovered them? Explain your answer.
items.a: There is no single right answer. Local people knew them first and used their glow. Scientists described them for the rest of the world and studied them. Both kinds of knowing matter, and both deserve credit.
items.why: This question is about fairness and how we know things. Any thoughtful answer with a reason is good.

items.p: Draw a deep-sea scene with three animals. Give each one a light with a different job: catch, hide, scare or talk. Label the jobs.
items.a: For example, an anglerfish with a lure (catch), a hatchetfish with belly lights (hide), and a jellyfish flashing a ring (scare).
items.why: Each glow should match a real job that light does in the dark sea.

items.p: Why do glowing mushrooms look plain and brown in the daytime?
opts: Their faint glow is still there, but sunlight is far brighter
They stop being alive in the day
They soak up the glow back inside
items.why: A faint light is hard to see next to a bright one. In the dark, the same faint glow stands out. Picking 'stop being alive' misses that the mushroom lives day and night. Some fungi do glow dimmer by day, but it is mostly the sunlight hiding them.

items.p: Sea sparkle glows most where waves crash, because it flashes when the water is stirred.
items.why: True. Sea sparkle flashes when it is disturbed, so the brightest glow is in breaking waves and around moving feet.

experiments.title: Warm Glow, Cold Glow: does warmth change a glow stick?
experiments.context: This is the glow stick test. You put glow sticks in cold, room-temperature and warm water, then compare how bright they glow. A glow stick makes light with a chemical reaction, a bit like a firefly does.
experiments.question: Does a glow stick glow brighter in cold water or in warm water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the glow stick in warm water be brighter, dimmer or the same as the one in cold water? Say why.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only one thing: how warm the water is. Use three glow sticks of the same colour and size, from the same packet. Snap them at the same moment. Use the same amount of water in the same kind of glass.
results_table: Still glowing next morning? (yes or no)

materials.item: 3 glow sticks of the same colour and size
3 steel tumblers or clear glasses
ice cubes and cold water
warm water from a tap or a kettle, cooled until it is comfortable for a hand
a dark room or a bathroom with the light off

experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the warm water. It should be warm like a bath, never boiling. Never cut or bite a glow stick. If one leaks, wash hands and do not touch eyes.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up three glasses. Snap the glow sticks and drop them in. Compare the glow in the dark. Check again next morning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Rank the brightness 1, 2 and 3. Next morning, write whether each one still glows.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers in a row: one with ice cubes, one with plain water, one with gently steaming warm water.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three glasses: icy, room temperature and warm.

setup.art: A child's hands bending three glow sticks at the same time until they click.
setup.caption: 2. Snap all three glow sticks together. Drop one into each glass.

setup.art: In a dark room, three glasses glowing: the warm one bright, the middle one medium, the icy one dim.
setup.caption: 3. Switch off the light. Which glows brightest?

flow.do: Show your child a glow stick. Do not snap it yet. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: This is a glow stick. Inside is a thin glass tube with one liquid, floating in another liquid. When I bend it, the tube cracks, the liquids mix, and they react. That makes light. A firefly makes light by mixing chemicals too. Do you think warm or cold will make the glow brighter?
flow.kid: Look at the glow stick. Inside are two liquids, kept apart. Bend it and they mix. Then it glows! Guess: brighter in warm water, or in cold?
flow.context: This is the first step of the glow stick test. You find out whether warm or cold water changes how bright a glow stick shines.

flow.do: 1. Put ice and cold water in the first glass. 2. Room-temperature water in the second. 3. Warm water in the third. 4. Fill all three to the same height.
flow.say: Let's fill three glasses to the same height. One icy, one normal, one warm, like a bath. Feel each one with a finger.
flow.kid: Help fill three glasses to the same height. One icy. One normal. One warm, for a grown-up to pour. Feel each with one finger.
flow.parent: Bath-warm is enough, about as warm as you would wash a baby in. Never use boiling water.

flow.do: Snap all three glow sticks at the same moment. Shake them. Drop one into each glass. Wait 2 minutes.
flow.say: On three, we all bend our sticks till they click. One, two, three! Shake them, and drop one in each glass. Now we wait two minutes, so the water can warm or cool them.
flow.kid: Bend all three sticks at once till they click. Shake them. Drop one in each glass. Wait two minutes.
flow.parent: Snapping them together matters. If one started earlier, the test would not be fair.

flow.do: Switch off the light. Look at the three glasses. Rank them 1, 2 and 3 for brightness. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Lights off! Which is brightest? Which is dimmest? Let's give them a number. 1 is the brightest.
flow.kid: Lights off! Look at the three glasses. Which is brightest? Give it a 1. Write it down.

check.q: In the glow stick test, which glass glowed brightest?
options: They were all exactly the same
check.why: Warmth makes the molecules inside move about faster. They bump into each other more often, so the reaction runs faster and gives out more light each second. Picking 'icy water' may come from thinking cold things shine, like ice glinting. Picking 'the same' may mean the room was not dark enough to see the difference. Try again in a darker room.

flow.do: Leave all three in their glasses overnight, away from children. Look again next morning in a dark bathroom.
flow.say: Let's leave them overnight. Tomorrow we'll see which one is still glowing. What do you guess?
flow.kid: Leave them overnight. Tomorrow, check in the dark. Which one still glows?
flow.parent: Usually the cold one still glows, and the warm one has almost run out. The warm one used up its chemicals faster. Bright and short, or dim and long.

check.q: Next morning, which glow stick was most likely still glowing?
options: The one from the icy water
The one from the warm water
None of them, glow sticks only last a minute
check.why: In the cold, the reaction runs slowly. The stick uses its chemicals slowly, so it lasts longer. The warm one burned through its chemicals fast. Picking 'warm' usually means thinking brighter means stronger, so it should last longer. In fact, brighter means it is spending faster.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: warmth makes a glow brighter but shorter. What I saw: the warm stick was brightest but was dark by morning, and the icy one still glowed. Why: warmth makes the chemicals react faster. Fireflies are the same. On cool nights, many fireflies flash more slowly.

experiments.title: Cold Light Test: is a glow hot?
experiments.context: This is the cold light test. You compare the warmth of a glowing glow stick with the warmth near a candle. Living light, like a firefly's, is cold light: it makes almost no heat.
experiments.question: Does a glow stick give out heat, the way a candle flame does?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will your hand feel warm near the glow stick? Will it feel warm near the candle?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, hold your hand the same distance from each light, about one hand-width away. Hold it there for the same time, a count of ten.
results_table: Hand one hand-width away: warm or not?
Thermometer next to it after 2 minutes (degrees), if you have one

materials.item: a glowing glow stick
a candle or a diya on a steel plate
matches, for a grown-up only
a kitchen or room thermometer, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights and watches the candle the whole time. Hold hands beside the candle, never over the flame. Tie back long hair.

schedule.what: Feel the warmth near a glow stick and near a candle. Measure with a thermometer if you have one.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the glow stick and the candle, with wavy heat lines where you felt heat.

setup.art: A lit diya on a steel plate and a glowing glow stick lying on a cloth, side by side on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Put a glowing glow stick and a lit candle side by side.

setup.art: A child's open hand held beside, not over, a diya flame, one hand-width away.
setup.caption: 2. Hold your hand one hand-width beside each one. Count to ten.

setup.art: Two small thermometers, one next to the glow stick, one next to the diya, the diya's reading higher.
setup.caption: 3. If you have a thermometer, check each one after 2 minutes.

flow.do: Light the candle. Put a glowing glow stick beside it, on a cloth.
flow.say: Both of these make light. One uses fire, one uses chemistry, like a firefly. Which do you think gives out heat?
flow.kid: Both of these make light. One is fire. One is chemistry, like a firefly. Which one is warm, do you think?
flow.context: This is the first step of the cold light test. You compare how warm a glow stick and a candle feel.

flow.do: Your child holds a hand one hand-width beside the glow stick for a count of ten. Then beside the candle. Never above the flame.
flow.say: Hold your hand next to the glow stick. Count to ten. Warm? Now the same next to the candle. Not above it, only beside it.
flow.kid: Hold your hand beside the glow stick. Count to ten. Now beside the candle, not above. Which felt warm?

check.q: Which one made your hand feel warm?
check.why: A flame turns a lot of its energy into heat. The glow stick turns its energy into light, with almost no heat. That is cold light. Picking 'the glow stick' may mean you held it, and your own hand warmed it. Picking 'both' usually means thinking all light is warm, like sunshine.

flow.do: If you have a thermometer, put it next to each light for 2 minutes and read it.
flow.say: Feelings can fool us. A thermometer cannot be fooled. Let's measure.
flow.kid: Put the thermometer next to each light. Wait two minutes. Read the number.
flow.parent: Near the glow stick, the reading should stay at room temperature. Near the candle, it rises. If you have no thermometer, skip this step.

flow.do: Blow out the candle. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you feel or measure? Why do you think a firefly needs cold light?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I felt. Why a firefly needs cold light.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer: The glow stick makes cold light. My hand felt warm by the candle but not by the glow stick. A firefly needs cold light because a hot light would burn its own body.

experiments.title: Made or Stored? Glow-in-the-dark stars
experiments.context: This test compares glow-in-the-dark stars with living light. A glow-in-the-dark star does not make light. It soaks up light, then gives it back slowly. You test whether shining a torch on it for longer makes it glow for longer.
experiments.question: If we shine a torch on a glow-in-the-dark star for longer, does it glow for longer in the dark?
experiments.predict: Guess. Will a star charged for 60 seconds glow longer than one charged for 10 seconds? How much longer?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use two stars from the same packet. Shine the same torch from the same distance. Change only how long you shine it. Time each star until you can no longer see it.

materials.item: 2 glow-in-the-dark stars from the same packet
a torch or a phone torch
a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
a dark room

experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

schedule.what: Keep both stars in the dark for an hour first. Charge one for 10 seconds and one for 60 seconds. Time how long each glows.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars, one for each star.

setup.art: Two glow-in-the-dark stars on a table, one under a torch beam, and a phone showing a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 1. Shine the torch on star A for 10 seconds. Shine it on star B for 60 seconds.

setup.art: A dark room with two faintly glowing stars, one brighter than the other, and a child watching.
setup.caption: 2. Switch off all lights. Start the stopwatch.

setup.art: A child pointing at the star that is still glowing while the other has faded.
setup.caption: 3. Stop the time when each star fades away.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: how long each star glowed after charging
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Keep both stars in a dark drawer for an hour before you start, so they are empty of light.
flow.say: These stars glow in the dark. A firefly makes its own light from food. Do you think these stars make their own light too? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Do glow-in-the-dark stars make their own light, like a firefly? Let's test them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the star test. You find out whether glow-in-the-dark stars make light or just give back light they soaked up.

ask.q: What would happen if we never shone any light on them?
good: Maybe they would still glow a little.

flow.do: Shine the torch on star A for 10 seconds, then on star B for 60 seconds. Keep the torch the same distance away.
flow.say: Star A gets ten seconds of torchlight. Star B gets sixty. Same torch, same distance.
flow.kid: Shine the torch on star A for 10 seconds. Then on star B for 60 seconds.

flow.do: Turn off the lights. Start the stopwatch. Note the time when each star fades so you can't see it.
flow.say: Lights off. Watch both stars. Tell me the moment each one disappears.
flow.kid: Lights off! Watch both stars. Shout when each one fades away.

check.q: In the star test, star B got 6 times more torchlight. What do you expect?
options: Both stop at exactly the same moment
check.why: A glow-in-the-dark star stores the light it soaks up, then lets it out slowly. More light in usually means more glow out. Picking 'star A' may come from thinking a short charge is fresher. Picking 'the same' means thinking the star makes its own light. It does not.

flow.do: Compare with a firefly. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: A firefly glows in the darkest night, with no torch at all. A star only gives back light it soaked up. What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: A firefly needs no torch. A star does. Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer: The stars do not make their own light. Star B glowed longer because it soaked up more light. A firefly is different, because it makes new light from food and oxygen.

check.q: Which one makes brand-new light of its own?
check.why: A firefly makes new light from a chemical reaction in its body. A glow-in-the-dark star only gives back light it soaked up. The Moon only sends back sunlight. Picking the star means mixing up 'glows in the dark' with 'makes light'. Both glow, but only one makes the light.

activities.title: Snap! A light with no switch
activities.context: This is a short way into the unit. In a dark room, you snap a glow stick and notice everything you can about its light. It works a bit like a firefly.

materials.item: 1 glow stick
a room you can make dark

activities.safety: Never cut or bite a glow stick.

schedule.what: Snap a glow stick in the dark. Notice and wonder.

activities.record: Write or say three things you noticed and two things you wonder.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding an unsnapped glow stick in both hands.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dark. Hold the glow stick.

setup.art: The glow stick bending with a small click, light spreading along it.
setup.caption: 2. Bend it till it clicks. Shake it.

setup.art: The child holding the glowing stick against a cheek, eyes wide.
setup.caption: 3. Notice everything. Touch it to your cheek. Is it warm?

flow.do: Make the room dark. Hand your child the glow stick, not yet snapped.
flow.say: Here's a stick with no battery, no wire and no flame. Let's see if it can make light.
flow.kid: Hold the stick. It has no battery and no wire. Can it make light?
flow.context: This is the first step of Snap!, a quick look at a light that needs no switch.

flow.do: Your child bends the stick till it clicks, then shakes it.
flow.say: Bend it till you hear a click. Shake it. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Bend it till it clicks. Shake it. What happens?

good: It got brighter when I shook it.

flow.do: Ask your child to hold it against a cheek, then look around the room by its light.
flow.say: Hold it to your cheek. Is it hot like a bulb? Now look around. What can you see by its light?
flow.kid: Hold it to your cheek. Is it hot? Look around the room by its glow.

check.q: You just held a glowing glow stick to your cheek. How did it feel?
options: Cool, about the same as the room
check.why: A glow stick makes light with a chemical reaction that makes almost no heat. This is called cold light. Fireflies make cold light too. Picking 'hot' usually means thinking all light comes with heat, like the Sun or a bulb. Picking 'cold like ice' may come from the word 'cold light', but it only means 'not hot'.

flow.do: Ask what your child wonders. Write down every question.
flow.say: What do you wonder about this light? Any question is a good question.
flow.kid: What do you wonder? Say every question you have.
flow.parent: Good wonderings: Where does the light come from? Will it run out? Can living things do this? Keep the list. The unit will answer many of them.

activities.title: Firefly Night Walk and Flash Count
activities.context: This is a night walk to look for fireflies, which are small beetles that flash light. You count how many flashes you see in one minute, in a dark place and near a bright light.

materials.item: a torch with a red cloth or red cellophane over it
a phone stopwatch or a watch
paper and pencil for tally marks

activities.safety: Go only with a grown-up. Wear closed shoes and long trousers. Watch for snakes near grass and water. Do not catch the fireflies.

schedule.what: After sunset, walk to a dark garden, park or field. Count flashes for one minute in two places.

activities.record: Make tally marks of flashes. Write the place and the time. Draw one firefly you saw.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child at the edge of a dark field at dusk, the torch covered with red cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Go out after sunset with a grown-up. Cover the torch with red cloth.

setup.art: A child making tally marks on paper while tiny flashes dot the dark grass.
setup.caption: 2. Stand still for one minute. Make a tally mark for each flash.

setup.art: The same child near a bright lamp post, with only one or two flashes in the dark beyond.
setup.caption: 3. Count again for one minute near a bright light. Compare.

flow.do: Choose a dark place: a garden, a park, a field edge. Go after sunset. Cover your torch with red cloth.
flow.say: We're going firefly spotting. We'll keep our torch dim and red, so our light doesn't drown theirs.
flow.kid: Go out with a grown-up after sunset. Keep the torch dim and red. Bright light hides firefly flashes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the firefly night walk. Fireflies are most common on warm, damp nights before and during the monsoon.
flow.parent: In much of India, fireflies are easiest to see from late May to July, around the first rains. If you see none, that is a real result too. Write it down.

flow.do: Stand still in the darkest spot for one minute. Your child makes a tally mark for every flash.
flow.say: Let's stand very still. For one minute, make a mark for every flash you see.
flow.kid: Stand still. For one minute, make a mark for each flash.

flow.do: Walk to a spot near a bright street light or porch light. Count for one minute again.
flow.say: Now let's try right next to the bright light. Count again for one minute.
flow.kid: Now count again near a bright light. One minute.

check.q: Where did you probably count more firefly flashes?
options: Always exactly the same in both
check.why: Fireflies flash to find each other. Near bright lights, their flashes are hard to see, and many fireflies stop flashing or move away. Picking 'next to the bright light' may come from moths, which fly to lamps. Fireflies are different. If your counts were the same, that is fine. Try on another night.

flow.do: Watch one firefly closely. Does it flash in a pattern? Is it flying or sitting still?
flow.say: Let's watch just one firefly. How many flashes in a row? How long between them?
flow.kid: Watch one firefly. Count its flashes. Is it flying, or sitting on a leaf?
flow.parent: Flying ones are often males, flashing their code. Ones sitting low on leaves are often females, answering.

flow.do: At home, ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think about fireflies and bright lights? What did you count? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I counted. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer: Bright lights are bad for fireflies. I counted 14 flashes in the dark spot and 2 near the lamp. Fireflies can't see each other's flashes in bright light.

activities.title: Shoebox Deep Sea
activities.context: In this activity you make a model of the deep sea inside a dark shoebox. The deep sea is the part of the ocean that sunlight never reaches. You add creatures that make their own light.

materials.item: a shoebox with a lid
black paper or paint
glow-in-the-dark paint or glow-in-the-dark stars
a small glow stick
white card, scissors, thread and sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors and makes the peephole.

schedule.what: Paint the box black. Make deep-sea creatures. Add their lights. Look through the peephole in the dark.

activities.record: Label each creature with its light job: catch, hide, scare or talk.

setup.art: A shoebox lying on its side, painted black inside, with a small hole cut in one end.
setup.caption: 1. Paint the inside of the box black. A grown-up cuts a peephole.

setup.art: Cut-out card fish, jellyfish and an anglerfish hanging on threads, with dots of glow paint on them.
setup.caption: 2. Make creatures from card. Paint only their light spots with glow paint.

setup.art: An eye at the peephole, and inside the box tiny glowing dots and a glowing anglerfish lure.
setup.caption: 3. Charge the paint with a torch, close the lid and peep in.

flow.do: Paint the inside of the box and lid black. A grown-up cuts a coin-sized peephole in one end.
flow.say: Deep in the sea, below about a thousand metres, it is black all day and all night. Let's make that darkness in a box.
flow.kid: Paint the inside of the box black. That is the deep sea. Ask a grown-up to cut a small peephole.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shoebox Deep Sea. You build a dark sea in a box and fill it with glowing creatures.

flow.do: Your child draws and cuts out 3 to 5 deep-sea animals. Add glow paint only where each animal makes light.
flow.say: Let's make an anglerfish, a jellyfish and a hatchetfish. Where does each one glow? Paint only those parts.
flow.kid: Make 3 to 5 sea creatures from card. Paint glow dots only where each one glows.
flow.parent: The anglerfish glows on the ball dangling in front of its mouth. The hatchetfish glows along its belly. A jellyfish can glow in a ring. Lanternfish have rows of dots along their sides.

flow.do: Hang the creatures from the lid with thread and tape. Shine a torch on them for a minute, then close the box.
flow.say: Let's hang them up. Now give them a minute of torchlight to charge the paint.
flow.kid: Hang them from the lid with thread. Shine a torch on them. Close the lid.

flow.do: Your child looks in through the peephole in a dark room.
flow.say: Peep in. What can you see? What can't you see?
flow.kid: Look through the hole. You can only see the glowing parts!

check.q: Our paint glows because we shone a torch on it. Real deep-sea animals have no torch. Where does their light come from?
options: They make it with chemistry in their bodies
From sunlight reaching the deep sea
check.why: Deep-sea animals make light with luciferin and oxygen, or with glowing bacteria they keep. Our paint only stores torchlight. Picking 'sunlight' misses that sunlight never reaches the deep sea. Picking 'the Moon' misses that moonlight is only sunlight bounced off the Moon, and it cannot reach the deep sea either.

activities.title: The Vanishing Fish: hiding with belly lights
activities.context: This activity shows how some sea animals hide by glowing. Seen from below, a fish looks like a dark shape against the light from above. A light on its belly can make that shape disappear.

materials.item: a fish shape cut from thin white paper, about the size of your palm
a phone or tablet showing a plain white screen, turned to low brightness
a small torch

activities.safety: Keep the torch pointed away from eyes.

schedule.what: Hold a paper fish against a glowing screen. Make its shape vanish with a torch from the front.

activities.record: Draw the fish before and after. Write: from below, a dark fish shows up because...

setup.art: A paper fish held flat against a dim glowing white screen in a dark room, showing as a darker shape.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the paper fish flat on a dim glowing screen. See its dark shape.

setup.art: A child shining a small torch onto the front of the same paper fish.
setup.caption: 2. Shine a small torch on the front of the fish.

setup.art: The paper fish almost invisible against the screen, its outline barely there.
setup.caption: 3. Move the torch nearer or further until the fish nearly vanishes.

flow.do: In a dim room, put the phone on a table with a white screen at low brightness. Lay the paper fish flat on the screen. Look from straight above.
flow.say: Pretend you are a hungry fish deep in the sea, looking up. The screen is the faint light from far above. What does our little fish look like?
flow.kid: Look down at the fish on the screen. You are a hungry fish looking up. Can you see the little fish?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Vanishing Fish. You find out how a fish can hide by glowing on its belly.

flow.do: Your child shines the torch onto the fish from above, moving it closer and further until the fish is as bright as the screen.
flow.say: Now let's give our fish belly lights. Shine the torch on it. Move the torch until the fish matches the screen.
flow.kid: Shine the torch on the fish. Move it closer or further. Can you make the fish disappear?

check.q: Why did the fish nearly disappear?
options: It became just as bright as the light behind it
check.why: We see a shape when it is darker or brighter than what is behind it. When the fish matches the background, its outline is gone. Real hatchetfish make their belly glow just as bright as the light from above. Picking 'see-through' is a good guess, but the paper did not change. Only its brightness did.

flow.do: Talk about real animals.
flow.say: In the sea, a fish with belly lights is hard to spot from below. Hunters looking up see nothing. Isn't it strange that light can help you hide?
flow.kid: Real hatchetfish do this. Their bellies glow. Hunters below can't see them.
flow.think: On land, a light shows people where you are. Why is it different in the dark sea?

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer: Belly lights help a fish hide. Our fish nearly vanished when the torch made it as bright as the screen. A hunter below can't see a shape that matches the light above.

activities.title: Deep Sea Theatre: act out the glowing jobs
activities.context: This is a short play in a dim room. Family members act as deep-sea animals and use torches or glow sticks for their lights. Deep-sea animals glow to catch food, hide, scare attackers and talk.

materials.item: 2 or 3 glow sticks or small torches
a dim room

activities.safety: Clear the floor so nobody trips in the dim light.

schedule.what: Act out three short deep-sea scenes with lights.

setup.art: A family in a dim living room, one person holding a glow stick on a string in front of their face like an anglerfish lure.
setup.caption: 1. Scene 1: the anglerfish dangles its lure. A small fish swims close.

setup.art: A child crouched low, holding a glow stick under their tummy, while a grown-up looks up from the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Scene 2: the hidden fish glows on its belly.

setup.art: A child whirling a glow stick in a circle while a 'shrimp' tiptoes away.
setup.caption: 3. Scene 3: the jellyfish flashes its burglar alarm.

flow.do: Scene 1. One person is an anglerfish, dangling a glow stick on a string in front of their mouth. Another is a small fish.
flow.say: The anglerfish waits in the dark, very still. Only its lure glows. Little fish, swim towards the light!
flow.kid: Be a little fish. You see a light! Swim close. Oh no, it's an anglerfish!
flow.context: This is the first step of Deep Sea Theatre. You act out how deep-sea animals use light.

flow.do: Scene 2. One person lies on the floor as a hunter looking up. Another walks past holding a glow stick under their belly.
flow.say: Hunter, look up. Can you see the shape of the fish going past? The fish is glowing on its belly to hide.
flow.kid: Hold the glow stick under your tummy. Walk past the hunter. Glowing helps you hide!

flow.do: Scene 3. A hungry shrimp grabs a jellyfish. The jellyfish whirls its glow stick in a circle. A big fish arrives.
flow.say: The jellyfish is caught! It flashes a ring of lights. That calls a bigger fish. Shrimp, run!
flow.kid: You are a jellyfish. When the shrimp grabs you, spin your light in a circle. Call for help!

check.q: In scene 3, why does the jellyfish flash when it is grabbed?
options: The flashes may call a bigger hunter to eat the attacker
To say hello to its friends
check.why: Scientists call this a burglar alarm. The flashes may bring a bigger animal that eats the shrimp. Picking 'light up its dinner' mixes it up with a lure. Picking 'say hello' mixes it up with talking signals. Each glow has its own job.

flow.do: Swap roles and play the scene each child liked best.
flow.say: Which job did your light have in each scene? Catch, hide or scare?
flow.kid: Swap parts. Say which job your light had.

projects.title: Firefly Count for Science
projects.context: In this 3-night project, you count fireflies in the same place, at the same time, on three evenings. Scientists need counts like this to know if fireflies are disappearing.

materials.item: a notebook for a firefly diary
a phone stopwatch or a watch
a torch covered with red cloth

projects.safety: Go only with a grown-up. Wear closed shoes. Stay on paths, away from water edges.

schedule.what: Choose a spot. Count flashes for 3 minutes, 30 minutes after sunset. Write the weather.
Same spot, same time. Count for 3 minutes. Write the weather.
Count again. Make a bar chart of your three nights. Ask a grandparent how many fireflies they saw as a child.

projects.record: Each night write the date, time, weather and your count. On night 3, draw a bar chart.

setup.art: A child and a parent marking a spot with a stone at the edge of a garden at dusk.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one spot and mark it. Come back at the same time each night.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and stopwatch, making tally marks, tiny flashes in the bushes.
setup.caption: 2. Count flashes for 3 minutes. Write the weather.

setup.art: A notebook page with three bars for three nights, and a grandmother pointing at it.
setup.caption: 3. After 3 nights, draw a bar chart. Ask a grandparent what they remember.

flow.do: Choose a dark spot near home where you might see fireflies. Mark it. Decide the time: about 30 minutes after sunset.
flow.say: Scientists want to know if fireflies are disappearing. To find out, they need careful counts. We can help. We'll count in the same place, at the same time, for three nights.
flow.kid: You are a firefly scientist. Pick one spot. Come back at the same time for three nights.
flow.context: This is the first step of the firefly count project. You count fireflies on three nights to see how their numbers change.
flow.parent: Same place and same time make the counts fair. The best season is late May to July. If you see no fireflies at all, record zero. A zero is also data.

flow.do: Each night, count flashes for 3 minutes. Write the count, the weather and whether the Moon was out.
flow.say: Three minutes, starting now. Mark every flash. Is it warm or cool tonight? Is it damp?
flow.kid: Count every flash for 3 minutes. Write the number. Is it warm, cool, wet or dry?
flow.wait: Repeat on the next two evenings

flow.do: On night 3, draw a bar chart with one bar for each night.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each night. Which night had the most? What was different that night?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each night. Which night had the most flashes? Why, do you think?

chart.title: Made-up example: firefly flashes counted in 3 minutes
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: In this made-up example from the firefly count, which night had the most flashes?
check.why: Night 3 has the tallest bar, 31 flashes. Fireflies are often busier on warm, damp nights. Picking night 2 may mean reading the shortest bar as the biggest. The taller the bar, the more flashes.

flow.do: Ask a grandparent or older neighbour how many fireflies they saw as a child, and where.
flow.say: Let's ask Nani or Dada. Were there more fireflies when you were young? Where did you see them?
flow.kid: Ask a grandparent. Did they see more fireflies when they were small? Where?
flow.parent: Many people say there were more fireflies before. Memories are useful clues, but they are not careful counts. That is why your counts matter.
flow.think: Is a grandparent's memory good evidence? How could we find out for sure if fireflies are disappearing?

flow.do: Write a short report: where, when, what you counted and what you think.
flow.say: Let's write a short science report. What do you think? What did you count? Why?
flow.kid: Write your report. What I think. What I counted. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good report: Fireflies like warm, damp nights. I counted 31 flashes after the rain and 9 on the cool windy night. Fireflies may flash more when it is warm and wet. Firefly scientists around the world collect counts like these. Ask if a local nature group collects them.

challenges.title: Invent a Deep-Sea Creature
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a new animal for the dark deep sea. It must use its own light to catch food without being eaten.
challenges.problem: Design an animal that lives 2,000 metres down, where it is always dark. It must find food and stay safe, using light it makes itself.
constraints: Its light must be cold light, made by chemistry, not fire.
It may glow in no more than three places.
Each light must have a job: catch, hide, scare or talk.
Sunlight never reaches it, so it cannot use colours that need sunlight to be seen.
materials: a glow stick or glow paint, for a model
clay or card, if you want to build it
general: Give it a glowing lure near its mouth, like an anglerfish.
Give it belly lights to hide its shape from hunters below.
Let it squirt glowing liquid to escape, like some shrimp.
creative: Give it lights that blink in a code only its own kind knows.
Let it keep glowing bacteria in a pocket, and switch them off with a flap of skin, like a flashlight fish.
Let it flash a burglar alarm that calls a bigger hunter.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own creature. Give it a name. Label each light and its job. Then build it from clay or card, and test it in the Shoebox Deep Sea.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a sketch of an odd fish, and small arrows pointing to three glowing spots.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your creature. Mark where it glows.

setup.art: Labels next to each glowing spot, shown as small pictures: a fish hook, an eye with a slash, a lightning bolt, two speech bubbles.
setup.caption: 2. Give each light a job: catch, hide, scare or talk.

setup.art: A clay model of the creature with glow-paint spots inside a dark shoebox.
setup.caption: 3. Build it and test it in the dark.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about the four jobs light can do in the deep sea.
flow.say: Down at 2,000 metres, it is black all the time. Your animal needs food and needs to stay safe. Its only tool is light it makes itself.
flow.kid: Your animal lives deep in the dark sea. It needs food. It must not be eaten. It can glow.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Invent a Deep-Sea Creature challenge. You design an animal that uses its own light.

flow.do: Your child draws the creature and marks up to three lights.
flow.say: Draw your creature. Where will it glow? Remember, no more than three lights.
flow.kid: Draw your animal. Mark up to three glowing spots.

flow.do: For each light, your child says or writes its job and how it works.
flow.say: Tell me about each light. Is it for catching, hiding, scaring or talking? How does it work?
flow.kid: For each light, say its job. Catch, hide, scare or talk? How does it work?

check.q: Your creature has bright lights all over its back. A hunter swims below it. Is it well hidden?
options: Not really. Belly lights hide you from hunters below
Yes, back lights hide you from below
check.why: Hunters below see your underside against the faint light from above. So hiding lights must be on the belly. Back lights would show to hunters above. Picking 'light can never help hiding' is natural on land. In the deep sea, belly lights are a real way to hide.

flow.do: Build it if there is time, and test it in the dark.
flow.say: Let's build it and switch off the lights. Does it look the way you hoped?
flow.kid: Build your animal. Test it in the dark. What would you change?

challenges.title: Light the Path, Save the Fireflies
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about light pollution. Light pollution is too much light at night where it is not needed. It stops fireflies from finding each other.
challenges.problem: A path through a park needs light, so people can walk home safely at night. But fireflies live in the park. Design lighting that keeps people safe and leaves the fireflies in the dark.
constraints: People must be able to see the path and their feet.
The fireflies' bushes and grass must stay as dark as possible.
Test your design on a model with torches and a toy path.
materials: a strip of paper for a path, on the floor
paper cups, foil or card to make shades
a few glow-in-the-dark stars or glow sticks, for 'fireflies'
general: Use shades so lights point down at the path only.
Use fewer, dimmer lights, low to the ground.
Switch lights off late at night, or use lights that turn on only when someone walks by.
creative: Mark the path edges with glow-in-the-dark stones or paint that need no electricity.
Use warm, dim lamps instead of bright white ones.
Leave a dark 'firefly corner' in every park.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own park lighting. Draw it. Build it with cups and torches. Can you keep the path bright and the firefly corner dark?

setup.art: A paper path on a dark floor with glow-in-the-dark stars scattered in a 'bush' area beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out a paper path and a firefly bush with glowing stars.

setup.art: A torch shining sideways and flooding the whole area, stars no longer visible.
setup.caption: 2. Shine an open torch. Can you still see the 'fireflies'?

setup.art: A torch inside a paper cup shade, pointing straight down at the path, stars glowing again in the dark beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Add a shade so light points only down at the path.

flow.do: Lay out the paper path and put the glow stars or glow sticks a little way beside it, as fireflies. Darken the room.
flow.say: These glowing stars are our fireflies. The paper is a path. People need light to walk here. Fireflies need dark to see each other.
flow.kid: The stars are fireflies. The paper is a path. People need light. Fireflies need dark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light the Path. You design lights that keep a path safe without hurting fireflies.

flow.do: Hold an unshaded torch above the path, shining all around. Look at the fireflies.
flow.say: Here's an ordinary lamp. What happens to our fireflies?
flow.kid: Shine the torch all around. Can you still see the fireflies?

check.q: In the Light the Path test, the open torch lit up everything. What happened to the 'fireflies'?
check.why: A bright light around them drowns out their faint glow. Real fireflies are harmed the same way, because they cannot see each other's flashes. Picking 'glowed brighter' may come from glow stars charging up in light. But we cannot see them while the torch floods the area.

flow.do: Your child designs shades from cups, foil or card, and tests them.
flow.say: Make a shade so the light only lands on the path. Test it. Can you see the fireflies now?
flow.kid: Make a shade from a cup or card. Point the light down. Test it.

flow.do: Compare designs and pick the best.
flow.say: Which design kept the path brightest and the firefly bush darkest? Why?
flow.kid: Which design worked best? Why?
flow.think: Where near our home is there a light that shines where nobody needs it?

opts: Light a living thing makes itself, with chemistry
Sunlight bouncing off a living thing
quiz.why: Living light is made by the living thing itself. Picking 'sunlight bouncing off' mixes up making light with sending back light.

quiz.p: Which of these makes its own light?
quiz.why: A firefly makes light with chemistry. The Moon, a mirror and a shirt only send back light from the Sun or a lamp. Picking the Moon is very common, because the Moon looks bright, but its light is borrowed sunlight.

quiz.p: Where do glowing mushrooms usually grow?
opts: On rotting wood in damp forests
On the tops of mountains in snow
quiz.why: Glowing fungi grow on damp, rotting wood, like the fallen bamboo near Mawlynnong in Meghalaya. Picking 'deep sea' mixes them up with glowing fish.

quiz.p: Where on Earth do the most glowing animals live?
opts: In the sea, especially the deep sea
quiz.why: In the deep sea, about three out of four animals can make light. Picking 'cities' may come from all the lamps there, but those are not living lights.

quiz.p: What does a firefly need from the air to make light?
quiz.why: Luciferin reacts with oxygen to make light. Picking 'sunlight' mixes the firefly up with glow-in-the-dark stars, which need light first.

quiz.p: You gently hold a glowing firefly. How does its light feel?
quiz.why: Living light is cold light. It makes almost no heat. Picking 'hot' usually means thinking all light comes with heat.

quiz.p: An anglerfish's glowing lure is used to…
quiz.why: Small fish swim to the light and are eaten. Picking 'see the sea floor' treats the lure as a headlamp.

quiz.p: A hatchetfish has lights on its belly. They help it…
opts: Hide its dark shape from hunters below
quiz.why: Belly lights match the faint light from above, so the fish's dark outline vanishes. Picking 'catch food' mixes it up with a lure.

quiz.p: In the glow stick test, one glow stick was in icy water and one in warm water. Which glowed brighter?
quiz.why: Warmth makes the chemicals react faster, so more light comes out. Picking 'the icy one' may come from thinking cold things shine.

quiz.p: To make the glow stick test fair, what must be different between the glasses?
opts: Only how warm the water is
The colour of each glow stick
quiz.why: A fair test changes just one thing. If the colours or glasses were different too, we would not know what caused the change. Picking 'everything' is a common first idea. Then we could never tell which change mattered.

quiz.p: A glow-in-the-dark star stops glowing after a while. Why?
opts: It has given back all the light it soaked up
quiz.why: Glow-in-the-dark stars only store light. When the stored light is used up, they go dark, until a light charges them again. Picking 'ran out of oxygen' mixes it up with living light, which needs oxygen.

opts: A firefly makes new light, but a glow-in-the-dark star only gives back stored light
Both only give back stored light
quiz.why: The firefly uses a chemical reaction. The star stores light from a torch or the Sun. Picking 'both make new light' mixes up glowing with making light.

quiz.p: What do bright lights at night do to fireflies?
opts: Hide their flashes, so they find fewer partners
quiz.why: Bright lights drown out faint firefly flashes. Picking 'help them see' may come from moths, which fly to lights. Fireflies are different.

opts: Scientists are still not sure. One idea is that the glow brings insects that spread spores
quiz.why: For one Brazilian mushroom, tests show the glow brings insects. For most other fungi, nobody knows yet. Picking 'to find partners' gives fungi eyes they do not have.

applications: Glow sticks, used for safety at night, in camping, at sea and at celebrations, work by the same kind of chemistry as fireflies.
Hospitals and food factories use firefly chemicals in swab tests. The swab glows if germs or food bits are left on a surface.
Scientists attach the green glowing protein from a jellyfish to parts of cells, to watch them grow and move.
Doctors and scientists use glowing chemicals to test new medicines on cells in the lab.
Engineers study firefly lanterns to design LED lights that waste less energy as heat.
Scientists have put mushroom glow genes into plants, which glow faintly. One day, plants might light paths.
Glowing bacteria are used to test whether water has harmful chemicals in it. If the bacteria dim, something is poisoning them.
Deep-sea scientists use fake glowing lures, like Edith Widder's e-jelly, to bring shy animals to their cameras.
Sailors have long known that glowing plankton can show the trail of a ship or a submarine at night.
Firefly festivals in Maharashtra bring visitors and money to villages that protect their forests.
Lighting designers make park and beach lights that point down and stay dim, to protect fireflies and turtles.
Glow-in-the-dark exit signs and paint help people find their way out in a power cut.

open_questions.q: How does a firefly switch its light on and off so fast?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know oxygen is let in and shut off. Exactly how the firefly controls this in a fraction of a second is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How do thousands of fireflies flash at exactly the same moment?
open_questions.why_open: Each firefly seems to watch its neighbours and adjust. Scientists build computer models, but how real fireflies do it is not fully known.

open_questions.q: Why do most glowing mushrooms glow?
open_questions.why_open: For one Brazilian mushroom, the glow brings insects. For many others, nobody has tested it.

open_questions.q: How did living light first begin in each group of living things?
open_questions.why_open: It began separately many times. Nobody was there to see, and old glowing animals rarely leave fossils that show their light.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of glowing animals live in the deep sea?
open_questions.why_open: Most of the deep sea has never been visited. New glowing animals are found on almost every deep trip.

open_questions.q: Are India's fireflies disappearing, and how fast?
open_questions.why_open: There are very few long, careful counts of fireflies in India. Scientists need many more people counting, in the same places, year after year.

open_questions.q: Does the faint light given off by our bodies tell us anything useful about health?
open_questions.why_open: It has been measured, but it is so faint that scientists are only beginning to study it.

maths.problem: In the made-up firefly count, these were the flashes counted in 3 minutes: Night 1, 24. Night 2, 9. Night 3, 31. Look at the chart. Put the nights in order, from most flashes to fewest.
maths.explain: Compare the numbers. 31 is bigger than 24, and 24 is bigger than 9. So Night 3 had the most, then Night 1, then Night 2. On the chart, the tallest bar is Night 3 and the shortest is Night 2.
maths.context: This is about the firefly count project. You count firefly flashes for 3 minutes, at the same place and time, on three nights.

chart.title: Made-up example: firefly flashes counted in 3 minutes

maths.why_maths: A list of counts is hard to read. Putting them in order shows straight away which night the fireflies liked best.

maths.problem: On the night walk, you counted 12 firefly flashes in 1 minute in the dark spot, and 3 flashes in 1 minute next to a bright lamp. How many times more flashes did you see in the dark?
maths.explain: In the dark spot there were 12 flashes. Near the lamp there were 3. 12 divided by 3 is 4. You can check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. So there were 4 times as many flashes in the dark.
maths.context: This is about the firefly night walk. You counted firefly flashes for one minute in a dark place, then one minute near a bright light.

chart.title: Made-up example: flashes counted in 1 minute

maths.why_maths: Saying '4 times more' tells us how big the effect of a bright light is, not just that there is one.

maths.problem: A firefly flashes once every 5 seconds. How many times does it flash in 1 minute?
maths.explain: One minute is 60 seconds. The firefly flashes once in every group of 5 seconds. 60 divided into groups of 5 makes 12 groups. Or count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. That is 12 fives. So it flashes 12 times.
maths.context: In many kinds of fireflies, the male flashes his code again and again, with the same gap each time. You watched this on the firefly night walk.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups lets a scientist work out a firefly's flash rate without counting for a whole minute.

maths.problem: In the star test, star A glowed for 90 seconds after 10 seconds of torchlight. Star B glowed for 270 seconds after 60 seconds of torchlight. Look at the chart. How many seconds longer did star B glow?
maths.explain: Star B glowed for 270 seconds. Star A glowed for 90 seconds. 270 take away 90 is 180. There are 60 seconds in a minute, and 60 + 60 + 60 = 180. So star B glowed 3 minutes longer.
maths.context: This is about the star test. You shone a torch on two glow-in-the-dark stars for different times, then timed how long each one glowed in the dark.

chart.title: Made-up example: how long each star glowed

maths.why_maths: Finding the difference between two times tells us how much the extra torchlight helped.

maths.problem: Sunlight fades as it goes down into the sea. At 200 metres it is dim. Below 1,000 metres it is completely dark. An anglerfish lives at 2,000 metres. How many metres below the start of the total darkness is it?
maths.explain: Total darkness starts at about 1,000 metres. The anglerfish lives at 2,000 metres. 2,000 take away 1,000 is 1,000. So it lives 1,000 metres below where the last light ends. That is about as deep as ten football fields laid end to end.
maths.context: This is about the deep sea, the part of the ocean that sunlight never reaches. You built a model of it in the Shoebox Deep Sea.

chart.title: How deep: from the dim sea to the anglerfish

maths.why_maths: Big numbers like thousands of metres are hard to picture. Subtracting them tells us how far into the dark the anglerfish really lives.

warmup.q: Light made by a living thing is called ____.
A firefly is a kind of fly. True or false?
warmup.a: False. A firefly is a beetle.

warmup.q: Which gas from the air does a firefly need to make light?
Is a firefly's light hot or cold?
warmup.a: Cold. It makes almost no heat.

warmup.q: Name one living thing that glows, apart from a firefly.
warmup.a: Any one: glowing mushrooms, jellyfish, anglerfish, lanternfish, sea sparkle, glowing bacteria.

warmup.q: Why does an anglerfish have a glowing lure?
warmup.a: To bring small fish close, so it can eat them.

warmup.q: Does a glow-in-the-dark star make its own light?
warmup.a: No. It gives back light it soaked up earlier.

warmup.q: Where on Earth do most glowing animals live?
warmup.a: In the sea, especially the deep sea.

warmup.q: What do bright lights at night do to fireflies?
warmup.a: They hide the fireflies' flashes, so they find fewer partners.

warmup.q: A glow stick in warm water glows brighter or dimmer?
warmup.a: Brighter, but it runs out sooner.

roots.context: We have been learning about living light: fireflies, mushrooms and sea animals that make their own glow. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Life is not only lit by light. Life can turn into light.
deep_truth.habit: We split the world into things that shine, like the Sun and lamps, and things that are only lit, like us. But a firefly turns its dinner into light, and so, very faintly, do you. The line between a light source and a living body is drawn by us.
deep_truth.evidence: Raphael Dubois mixed two juices from a glowing beetle in a tube, and they glowed. The energy in a firefly's food, which first came from sunlight, comes out again as light.

three.who_am_i: You are made of the same kind of chemistry that lights a firefly. Your body even glows, too faintly to see.
three.what_is_life: Life takes in sunlight, as food, and sometimes gives it back as light, to call a friend or light a path.
three.what_is_this_world: Even the darkest place on Earth, the deep sea, is full of small living lights.

roots.thread: The Sun pours out light. Plants catch it and turn it into food. A firefly eats, and turns that same energy into a flash. A mushroom, a jellyfish and a tiny plankton do it in their own ways. DeepKids believes this is the One showing up as many: one energy moving through many bodies, sometimes hidden, sometimes shining. Light that seemed to belong only to the Sun turns out to run through all of life.

teachings.teaching: There the Sun does not shine, nor the Moon and stars, nor lightning, let alone this fire. When That shines, everything shines after it. By its light, all this is lit.
teachings.link: The Upanishad points to a light behind every light. In science, the firefly's flash is the Sun's energy, passed on through plants and food, shining again in a new form.

teachings.source: The Buddha's last teaching, in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 16)
teachings.teaching: Be a lamp for yourselves. Be a refuge for yourselves. The Pali word 'dipa' can mean both lamp and island, and scholars translate it both ways.
teachings.link: A firefly or a glowing mushroom does not wait for the Sun. In the darkest places, life makes its own light.

science.text: Living light comes from a chemical reaction of luciferin with oxygen. The energy in the food that powers it first came from sunlight caught by plants.
Living light began separately at least 94 times in the history of life, as if life keeps finding its way to light again and again.

other_view.who: Many biologists, and the old Indian Charvaka school, who said only what we can sense and measure is real
other_view.view: A firefly's glow is chemistry that helped fireflies survive and have young. It needs no deeper meaning. There is no One behind it, only molecules and evolution. That is an honest and careful view.

practice.title: Sit with a small light
practice.say: Let's sit in the dark with one glow stick between us. Breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out while I count to four. Look softly at the glow. Now close your eyes. Can you still see a little light behind your eyelids? Sit quietly for a few breaths. Where do you think that light came from?
practice.kid: Sit in the dark with one glow stick. Breathe in for four. Breathe out for four. Look at the glow. Close your eyes. Is there still a little light inside?

ask: The energy in your breakfast came from the Sun. Is some of the Sun inside you now?
If a firefly turns food into light, what do you turn your food into?
The mushrooms glowed all along, but nobody saw them in daylight. What might be shining around us that we do not notice?
